title: Δόλων
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Diomedes and Odysseus, their prayer heard by Athena, go out like two lions through the dead. Hector calls the Trojan chiefs and offers a chariot and two strong-necked horses to the man who will go and learn what the Achaeans are doing at the ships. Dolon, the only son of a rich herald, ugly but fleet-footed, volunteers and has Hector swear that he shall have the horses of Achilles; the poet says the oath was false. Dolon puts on a wolfskin and a weasel-skin helmet and sets out. Odysseus sees him coming, and the two let him pass and then chase him down like hounds after a hare. Diomedes’ spear misses on purpose, and Dolon, pale and with his teeth chattering, offers a ransom. Odysseus bids him take courage and asks why he is out alone in the night.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαν εὐχόμενοι, τῶν δ’ ἔκλυε Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη.
sentences.tr: hōs ephan euchomenoi, tōn d’ eklye Pallas Athēnē.
sentences.l: So they spoke, praying, and Pallas Athena heard them.
sentences.i: So they prayed, and Pallas Athena heard them.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαν εὐχόμενοι ‘so they spoke, praying’ closes the double prayer of Diomedes and Odysseus at the end of the last part. ἔφαν is a past tense of φημί ‘say’, third person plural. τῶν ‘of them’ is the old demonstrative used as a pronoun, in the genitive that ἔκλυε ‘heard’ (aorist of κλύω) takes, and Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη is a fixed name pair. The line is the formula of a prayer that is heard, as for Apollo at 1.43. The edition begins a new paragraph here.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἐπεὶ ἠρήσαντο Διὸς κούρῃ μεγάλοιο,
βάν ῥ’ ἴμεν ὥς τε λέοντε δύω διὰ νύκτα μέλαιναν
ἂμ φόνον, ἂν νέκυας, διά τ’ ἔντεα καὶ μέλαν αἷμα.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ epei ērēsanto Dios kourēi megaloio,
ban rh’ imen hōs te leonte dyō dia nykta melainan
am phonon, an nekyas, dia t’ entea kai melan haima.
sentences.l:
And they, when they had prayed to the daughter of great Zeus,
set out to go, like two lions, through the black night,
up through slaughter, up through corpses, and through gear and black blood.
sentences.i: When they had prayed to the daughter of great Zeus, they set out like two lions through the black night, through the slaughter, through the corpses, through the gear and the black blood.
sentences.n: The subject is the pair, Diomedes and Odysseus. οἳ δ’ ἐπεὶ ἠρήσαντο is ‘and when they had prayed’, and Διὸς κούρῃ μεγάλοιο is the formula ‘to the daughter of great Zeus’, that is Athena. βάν is an aorist of βαίνω without augment, and βάν ῥ’ ἴμεν is the house ‘set out to go’ (ἴμεν = ἰέναι). λέοντε δύω is a dual, ‘two lions’, with δύω repeating the number. ἂμ and ἂν are ἀνά ‘up through’ shortened before φ and ν. ἔντεα is ‘gear’, the dead men’s equipment.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ μὲν οὐδὲ Τρῶας ἀγήνορας εἴασεν Ἕκτωρ
εὕδειν, ἀλλ’ ἄμυδις κικλήσκετο πάντας ἀρίστους,
ὅσσοι ἔσαν Τρώων ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες·
sentences.tr:
oude men oude Trōas agēnoras eiasen Hektōr
heudein, all’ amydis kiklēsketo pantas aristous,
hossoi esan Trōōn hēgētores ēde medontes·
sentences.i: Hector, for his part, would not let the proud Trojans sleep either, but called together all the best of them, all who were leaders and lords of the Trojans;
sentences.n: Hector too is awake. οὐδὲ μὲν οὐδέ ‘nor again … either’ is an emphatic negative that sets him beside the Achaeans, who are also up in the night. Τρῶας ἀγήνορας pairs the Trojans with ἀγήνωρ, ‘manly’ in the literal line and ‘proud’ in the free one, as in θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ. εἴασεν is the aorist of ἐάω ‘allow’; κικλήσκετο is an imperfect middle, ‘he kept summoning’. Τρώων ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες is the house ‘leaders and lords of the Trojans’. The unit ends at the raised dot (·).

sentences.t: τοὺς ὅ γε συγκαλέσας πυκινὴν ἀρτύνετο βουλήν·
sentences.tr: tous ho ge synkalesas pykinēn artyneto boulēn·
sentences.l: These, having called them together, he arranged a close-packed plan:
sentences.i: He called them together and set out a shrewd plan:
sentences.n: τοὺς ‘these’ are the leaders just named, and ὅ γε is ‘he, for his part’, Hector. συγκαλέσας is the aorist participle ‘having called together’, and ἀρτύνετο is an imperfect middle, ‘he arranged’. πυκινὴν βουλήν ‘a close-packed plan’ is the house rendering (‘shrewd plan’ in the free English). The line is word for word 2.55, where Agamemnon calls his council, and has the same English there. The colon leads into Hector’s speech.

sentences.t:
τίς κέν μοι τόδε ἔργον ὑποσχόμενος τελέσειε
δώρῳ ἔπι μεγάλῳ;
sentences.tr:
tis ken moi tode ergon hyposchomenos teleseie
dōrōi epi megalōi;
sentences.l:
“Who might this task, having undertaken it for me, accomplish
for a great gift?
sentences.i: “Who would undertake this task for me and see it through, for a great gift?
sentences.n: Hector speaks, and since the Greek has no quotation marks the unit before it names him. τίς κέν … τελέσειε is a question with κέν and the optative, ‘who would accomplish’. ὑποσχόμενος is the aorist middle participle of ὑπισχνέομαι, ‘having undertaken’ or ‘having promised’, and μοι is ‘for me’. δώρῳ ἔπι μεγάλῳ ‘for a great gift’ has ἔπι (= ἐπί) placed after its noun. The unit ends at the Greek question mark (;), which is the sign printed like a semicolon.

sentences.t: μισθὸς δέ οἱ ἄρκιος ἔσται.
sentences.tr: misthos de hoi arkios estai.
sentences.l: And for him the wage will be sufficient.
sentences.i: And the pay for him will be ample.
sentences.n: This sentence begins in the middle of line 304, after the question mark. μισθός is ‘wage’ or ‘pay’, οἱ is ‘for him’ (the man who takes the task), and ἔσται ‘will be’. ἄρκιος is usually taken as ‘sufficient’, from ἀρκέω ‘suffice’, but ‘sure’ or ‘assured’ is also given for it in the old lexica; ‘sufficient’ is the house choice, and the exact force is not certain.

sentences.t:
δώσω γὰρ δίφρόν τε δύω τ’ ἐριαύχενας ἵππους
οἵ κεν ἄριστοι ἔωσι θοῇς ἐπὶ νηυσὶν Ἀχαιῶν
ὅς τίς κε τλαίη, οἷ τ’ αὐτῷ κῦδος ἄροιτο,
sentences.tr:
dōsō gar diphron te dyō t’ eriauchenas hippous
hoi ken aristoi eōsi thoēis epi nēusin Achaiōn
hos tis ke tlaiē, hoi t’ autōi kydos aroito,
sentences.l:
For I shall give a chariot and two strong-necked horses,
whichever shall be the best at the swift ships of the Achaeans,
to whoever might bring himself, and for himself glory win,
sentences.i: For I shall give a chariot and two strong-necked horses, the best at the swift ships of the Achaeans, to the man who can bring himself to do it and win glory for himself,
sentences.n: δώσω γάρ ‘for I shall give’ says why the task is worth taking. δίφρον is ‘chariot’, and δύω … ἵππους ‘two horses’ carries ἐριαύχενας, a compound of an intensifying ἐρι- and αὐχήν ‘neck’; ‘strong-necked’ is a guess at it and its exact meaning is not known. οἵ κεν ἄριστοι ἔωσι ‘which may be the best’ (ἔωσι = ὦσι) describes the horses. ὅς τίς κε τλαίη ‘whoever might bring himself’ names the man, who is also to win κῦδος ‘glory’ (ἄροιτο ‘would win’). The infinitives that finish the thought follow in line 308.

sentences.t:
νηῶν ὠκυπόρων σχεδὸν ἐλθέμεν, ἔκ τε πυθέσθαι
ἠέ φυλάσσονται νῆες θοαὶ ὡς τὸ πάρος περ,
sentences.tr:
nēōn ōkyporōn schedon elthemen, ek te pythesthai
ēe phylassontai nēes thoai hōs to paros per,
sentences.l:
to come near the swift-faring ships, and to find out
whether the swift ships are guarded as before,
sentences.i: to come near the swift-faring ships and find out whether the swift ships are guarded just as before,
sentences.n: The infinitives ἐλθέμεν ‘to come’ (-έμεν = -ειν) and ἔκ τε πυθέσθαι ‘and to find out’ (a tmesis for ἐκπυθέσθαι) depend on τλαίη in the line before: they are what the man must dare. σχεδόν ‘near’ takes the genitive νηῶν ὠκυπόρων ‘the swift-faring ships’. ἠέ … ‘whether’ opens a double question that ἦ ‘or’ completes in line 310. φυλάσσονται is passive, ‘are guarded’, and ὡς τὸ πάρος περ is ‘just as before’.

sentences.t:
ἦ ἤδη χείρεσσιν ὑφ’ ἡμετέρῃσι δαμέντες
φύξιν βουλεύουσι μετὰ σφίσιν, οὐδ’ ἐθέλουσι
νύκτα φυλασσέμεναι, καμάτῳ ἀδηκότες αἰνῷ.
sentences.tr:
ē ēdē cheiressin hyph’ hēmeterēisi damentes
phyxin bouleuousi meta sphisin, oud’ ethelousi
nykta phylassemenai, kamatōi adēkotes ainōi.
sentences.l:
or whether, already beneath our hands overcome,
they are planning flight among themselves, and are unwilling
to keep watch through the night, worn out with fearsome weariness.”
sentences.i: or whether, overcome already beneath our hands, they are plotting flight among themselves and do not want to keep watch in the night, worn out by fearsome weariness.”
sentences.n: ἦ here is ‘or whether’, answering ἠέ in line 309, and is not ‘truly’. δαμέντες is the aorist passive participle of δαμάζω ‘overcome’, with χείρεσσιν ὑφ’ ἡμετέρῃσι ‘beneath our hands’. φύξιν βουλεύουσι is ‘they plan flight’, and μετὰ σφίσιν ‘among themselves’. νύκτα is ‘through the night’. ἀδηκότες is a perfect participle whose sense is not quite certain; ‘worn out’ is the usual guess. καμάτῳ αἰνῷ ‘with fearsome weariness’. Hector’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ.
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, hoi d’ ara pantes akēn egenonto siōpēi.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they then all became still in silence;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they all fell hushed and silent;
sentences.n: The formula that ends a speech and shows the hush that follows: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is ‘so he spoke’ (ἔφαθ’ = ἔφατο, cut short and aspirated before the rough breathing of οἳ), ἀκήν ‘hushed’ is an adverb, and σιωπῇ ‘in silence’ is a dative. The line is word for word 3.95 and takes the same English; there and here the English ends in a semicolon, though the edition prints a raised dot there and a full stop here. The edition begins a new paragraph.

sentences.t:
ἦν δέ τις ἐν Τρώεσσι Δόλων Εὐμήδεος υἱὸς
κήρυκος θείοιο πολύχρυσος πολύχαλκος,
ὃς δή τοι εἶδος μὲν ἔην κακός, ἀλλὰ ποδώκης·
sentences.tr:
ēn de tis en Trōessi Dolōn Eumēdeos huios
kērykos theioio polychrysos polychalkos,
hos dē toi eidos men eēn kakos, alla podōkēs·
sentences.i: Among the Trojans there was a man named Dolon, the son of Eumedes, the divine herald, rich in gold and rich in bronze; he was ugly to look at, but fleet-footed;
sentences.n: A new character comes in. ἦν δέ τις ‘there was one’; Δόλων is his name, and Εὐμήδεος υἱὸς … κήρυκος θείοιο ‘son of Eumedes, a divine herald’ gives his father (θεῖος ‘divine’ is the house word). πολύχρυσος πολύχαλκος ‘rich in gold, rich in bronze’ are two compounds. ὃς δή τοι ‘who, you see’ turns to his looks: εἶδος ‘form’ was κακός ‘bad’, meaning ugly, ἀλλὰ ποδώκης ‘but fleet-footed’. The unit ends at the raised dot (·).

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὃ μοῦνος ἔην μετὰ πέντε κασιγνήτῃσιν.
sentences.tr: autar ho mounos eēn meta pente kasignētēisin.
sentences.l: but he alone was among five sisters.
sentences.i: but he was the only son among five sisters.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὃ ‘but he’ goes on with the portrait. μοῦνος ‘alone, only’ is masculine, so he is the one son, and κασιγνήτῃσιν is the dative plural of κασιγνήτη ‘sister’ (the form in -ῃσιν is epic); the Greek does not say ‘son’, which is read from the masculine word set against five sisters. μετά with the dative is ‘among’.

sentences.t: ὅς ῥα τότε Τρωσίν τε καὶ Ἕκτορι μῦθον ἔειπεν·
sentences.tr: hos rha tote Trōsin te kai Hektori mython eeipen·
sentences.l: he then to the Trojans and to Hector spoke a word:
sentences.i: It was he who now spoke to the Trojans and to Hector:
sentences.n: ὅς ῥα τότε ‘who then’ takes Dolon up again, as the same opening does for a speaker in the Odyssey. Τρωσίν is the epic dative plural in -σιν, ‘to the Trojans’, and Ἕκτορι ‘to Hector’. μῦθον ἔειπεν is ‘spoke a word’; ἔειπεν is an epic form of εἶπεν.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορ ἔμ’ ὀτρύνει κραδίη καὶ θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ
νηῶν ὠκυπόρων σχεδὸν ἐλθέμεν ἔκ τε πυθέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
Hektor em’ otrynei kradiē kai thymos agēnōr
nēōn ōkyporōn schedon elthemen ek te pythesthai.
sentences.l:
“Hector, me urges on my heart and my manly spirit
to come near the swift-faring ships and to find out.
sentences.i: “Hector, my heart and my proud spirit urge me on to come near the swift-faring ships and find out.
sentences.n: Dolon speaks. The first line is Diomedes’ at 10.220 with a different name, and has the same English: ἔμ’ (= ἐμέ) ὀτρύνει κραδίη καὶ θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ ‘my heart and my manly spirit urge me on’, the verb singular after two subjects. The second line is Hector’s own words of line 308, νηῶν ὠκυπόρων σχεδὸν ἐλθέμεν ἔκ τε πυθέσθαι, and gets the same English: Dolon offers to do just what Hector asked.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι τὸ σκῆπτρον ἀνάσχεο, καί μοι ὄμοσσον
ἦ μὲν τοὺς ἵππους τε καὶ ἅρματα ποικίλα χαλκῷ
δωσέμεν, οἳ φορέουσιν ἀμύμονα Πηλεΐωνα,
σοὶ δ’ ἐγὼ οὐχ ἅλιος σκοπὸς ἔσσομαι οὐδ’ ἀπὸ δόξης·
sentences.tr:
all’ age moi to skēptron anascheo, kai moi omosson
ē men tous hippous te kai harmata poikila chalkōi
dōsemen, hoi phoreousin amymona Pēleïōna,
soi d’ egō ouch halios skopos essomai oud’ apo doxēs·
sentences.l:
But come, hold up the sceptre for me, and swear to me
that truly the horses and the chariot intricate with bronze
you will give, which carry the blameless son of Peleus,
and to you I shall be no lookout in vain, nor away from expectation;
sentences.i: But come, hold up the sceptre for me and swear to me that you will give me the horses, and the chariot intricately worked with bronze, that carry the blameless son of Peleus; and I shall not be a lookout in vain for you, nor fall short of what you expect;
sentences.n: Dolon asks for a pledge first. ἀνάσχεο is the middle imperative of ἀνέχω ‘hold up’ (Hector is to hold up the sceptre while he swears), and ὄμοσσον ‘swear’. ἦ μέν ‘truly’ opens what is to be sworn, with the infinitive δωσέμεν (= δώσειν) ‘that you will give’. The horses are Achilles’, ἀμύμονα Πηλεΐωνα ‘the blameless son of Peleus’; the meaning of ἀμύμων is not known, and ‘blameless’ is the house word. οὐχ ἅλιος σκοπός is ‘no lookout in vain’, and ἀπὸ δόξης ‘away from expectation’ is not certain in exact sense.

sentences.t:
τόφρα γὰρ ἐς στρατὸν εἶμι διαμπερὲς ὄφρ’ ἂν ἵκωμαι
νῆ’ Ἀγαμεμνονέην, ὅθι που μέλλουσιν ἄριστοι
βουλὰς βουλεύειν ἢ φευγέμεν ἠὲ μάχεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
tophra gar es straton eimi diamperes ophr’ an hikōmai
nē’ Agamemnoneēn, hothi pou mellousin aristoi
boulas bouleuein ē pheugemen ēe machesthai.
sentences.l:
For so long I shall go through the army, right through, until I come
to the ship of Agamemnon, where presumably the best are about
to plan plans, whether to flee or to fight.”
sentences.i: For I shall go right through the army until I reach the ship of Agamemnon, where the best men are presumably about to take counsel on whether to flee or to fight.”
sentences.n: τόφρα … ὄφρ’ ἂν ‘for so long … until’ gives the length of his errand, and διαμπερές is ‘right through’. νῆ’ is νῆα ‘ship’, and Ἀγαμεμνονέην is the adjective ‘of Agamemnon’. ὅθι που ‘where presumably’, and μέλλουσιν ‘are about to’. The last line, βουλὰς βουλεύειν ἢ φευγέμεν ἠὲ μάχεσθαι, is also 10.147 (Nestor, in the first part of the book), and takes the English of that line. Dolon’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς φάθ’, ὃ δ’ ἐν χερσὶ σκῆπτρον λάβε καί οἱ ὄμοσσεν·
sentences.tr: hōs phath’, ho d’ en chersi skēptron labe kai hoi omossen·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and he took the sceptre in his hands and swore to him:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Hector took the sceptre in his hands and swore to him:
sentences.n: ὣς φάθ’ ‘so he spoke’ (φάθ’ = φάτο, no augment) closes Dolon’s speech. ὃ δέ ‘and he’ is Hector, who takes the σκῆπτρον ‘sceptre’ as the object held for an oath, as Achilles swore by his at 1.234. λάβε is an aorist without augment, and ὄμοσσεν (= ὤμοσεν) the aorist of ὄμνυμι ‘swear’, with a doubled σ. οἱ is ‘to him’. The edition begins a new paragraph here.

sentences.t:
ἴστω νῦν Ζεὺς αὐτὸς ἐρίγδουπος πόσις Ἥρης
μὴ μὲν τοῖς ἵπποισιν ἀνὴρ ἐποχήσεται ἄλλος
Τρώων, ἀλλά σέ φημι διαμπερὲς ἀγλαϊεῖσθαι.
sentences.tr:
istō nyn Zeus autos erigdoupos posis Hērēs
mē men tois hippoisin anēr epochēsetai allos
Trōōn, alla se phēmi diamperes aglaïeisthai.
sentences.l:
“Let Zeus himself now know, the loud-crashing husband of Hera,
that on these horses no other man will ride
of the Trojans, but you, I say, right through will take splendour in them.”
sentences.i: “Let Zeus himself know it now, the loud-crashing husband of Hera: no other man of the Trojans will ride behind these horses, but you, I declare, will go on taking proud delight in them.”
sentences.n: Hector’s oath, with no quotation marks in the Greek. ἴστω is the imperative of οἶδα, ‘let him know’, Zeus being the witness, and ἐρίγδουπος πόσις Ἥρης ‘the loud-crashing husband of Hera’ is the house formula. μὴ μέν opens the thing sworn, ‘surely not’; ἐποχήσεται is a future, ‘will ride on’, with the dative ἵπποισιν. ἀγλαϊεῖσθαι is a future infinitive of a verb from ἀγλαΐη ‘splendour’, ‘to glory in, take pride in’; its exact nuance is not known. διαμπερές ‘right through’ is here a time word, ‘continually’.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο καί ῥ’ ἐπίορκον ἐπώμοσε, τὸν δ’ ὀρόθυνεν·
sentences.tr: hōs phato kai rh’ epiorkon epōmose, ton d’ orothynen·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and he swore a false oath, and him he roused;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and swore a false oath, and so roused him;
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο ‘so he spoke’ is the formula of line 313 in another form (φάτο = ἔφατο without augment). ἐπίορκον ἐπώμοσε is ‘swore a false oath’: ἐπίορκον is an adjective used as a noun, ‘a false oath’, ἐπώμοσε the aorist of ἐπόμνυμι ‘swear’. The poet calls the oath false as he reports it, before Dolon sets out. τὸν δ’ ὀρόθυνεν ‘and him he roused’ (ὀροθύνω ‘stir up, rouse’). The edition begins a new paragraph.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δ’ ἀμφ’ ὤμοισιν ἐβάλλετο καμπύλα τόξα,
ἕσσατο δ’ ἔκτοσθεν ῥινὸν πολιοῖο λύκοιο,
κρατὶ δ’ ἐπὶ κτιδέην κυνέην, ἕλε δ’ ὀξὺν ἄκοντα,
βῆ δ’ ἰέναι προτὶ νῆας ἀπὸ στρατοῦ·
sentences.tr:
autika d’ amph’ ōmoisin eballeto kampyla toxa,
hessato d’ ektosthen rhinon polioio lykoio,
krati d’ epi ktideēn kyneēn, hele d’ oxyn akonta,
bē d’ ienai proti nēas apo stratou·
sentences.l:
At once about his shoulders he threw the bent bow,
and clothed himself on the outside in the skin of a grey wolf,
and on his head a weasel-skin helmet, and took a sharp javelin,
and set out to go to the ships from the army;
sentences.i: At once he slung the bent bow about his shoulders, clothed himself on the outside in the skin of a grey wolf, put a weasel-skin helmet on his head, took a sharp javelin, and set out from the army for the ships;
sentences.n: Dolon arms himself. ἐβάλλετο is the imperfect middle of βάλλω ‘threw about himself’, and καμπύλα τόξα ‘the bent bow’ is a plural for one bow. ἕσσατο is the aorist middle of ἕννυμι ‘clothed himself’, ἔκτοσθεν ‘on the outside’, ῥινὸν πολιοῖο λύκοιο ‘the skin of a grey wolf’. κτιδέην is the adjective of κτίς, some small weasel-like animal (weasel, marten or polecat; which one is not known), and κυνέη is the house ‘helmet’. ὀξὺν ἄκοντα is ‘a sharp javelin’. The unit ends at the raised dot after στρατοῦ.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔμελλεν
ἐλθὼν ἐκ νηῶν ἂψ Ἕκτορι μῦθον ἀποίσειν.
sentences.tr:
oud’ ar’ emellen
elthōn ek nēōn aps Hektori mython apoisein.
sentences.l:
nor was he then destined,
having come from the ships, back to Hector a word to carry.
sentences.i: but he was never to come back from the ships and carry word to Hector.
sentences.n: The poet looks ahead. οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔμελλεν ‘and he was not then going’ has ἔμελλεν with the future infinitive ἀποίσειν ‘to carry back’, and it is used of what is fated, so Dolon will not bring Hector his report. ἐλθὼν ἐκ νηῶν ‘having come from the ships’, ἂψ ‘back’. The unit begins in the middle of line 336, after the raised dot.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ἵππων τε καὶ ἀνδρῶν κάλλιφ’ ὅμιλον,
βῆ ῥ’ ἀν’ ὁδὸν μεμαώς·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē rh’ hippōn te kai andrōn kalliph’ homilon,
bē rh’ an’ hodon memaōs·
sentences.l:
But when he had left behind the throng of horses and men,
he set out then along the way, eager;
sentences.i: But when he had left the throng of horses and men behind, he set out along the road, eager;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ‘but when’ is a common narrative opening. κάλλιφ’ is a shortened and elided form of κατέλιπε, ‘left behind’ (καταλείπω), and ἵππων τε καὶ ἀνδρῶν ὅμιλον ‘the throng of horses and men’ is the Trojan host with its teams. βῆ ῥ’ ἀν’ ὁδόν is ‘set out along the way’ (ἀνά with the accusative), and μεμαώς, a perfect participle, is ‘eager’. The unit ends at the raised dot in line 339.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ φράσατο προσιόντα
διογενὴς Ὀδυσεύς, Διομήδεα δὲ προσέειπεν·
sentences.tr:
ton de phrasato prosionta
diogenēs Odyseus, Diomēdea de proseeipen·
sentences.l:
and him noticed approaching
Zeus-sprung Odysseus, and addressed Diomedes:
sentences.i: Zeus-born Odysseus noticed him coming, and spoke to Diomedes:
sentences.n: τὸν δὲ φράσατο προσιόντα: τόν ‘him’ is Dolon, φράσατο the aorist middle of φράζομαι ‘notice’, and προσιόντα the accusative participle of πρόσειμι ‘approaching’. διογενής is ‘Zeus-sprung’ in the literal line and ‘Zeus-born’ in the free one. Διομήδεα is the accusative of Διομήδης, and προσέειπεν is an epic form of προσεῖπεν ‘addressed’. The unit begins in the middle of line 339.

sentences.t:
οὗτός τις Διόμηδες ἀπὸ στρατοῦ ἔρχεται ἀνήρ,
οὐκ οἶδ’ ἢ νήεσσιν ἐπίσκοπος ἡμετέρῃσιν,
ἦ τινα συλήσων νεκύων κατατεθνηώτων.
sentences.tr:
houtos tis Diomēdes apo stratou erchetai anēr,
ouk oid’ ē nēessin episkopos hēmeterēisin,
ē tina sylēsōn nekyōn katatethnēōtōn.
sentences.l:
“This, Diomedes, is some man coming from the army,
I do not know whether a scout for our ships,
or going to strip someone of the dead, of those who have died.
sentences.i: “Diomedes, here is a man coming from the army, and I do not know whether he is a scout for our ships or is on his way to strip one of the dead.
sentences.n: Odysseus speaks to Diomedes while Dolon is still a distance off. οὗτός τις … ἀνήρ is ‘this is some man’; οὐκ οἶδ’ ἢ … ἦ ‘I do not know whether … or’ sets out the two possibilities. ἐπίσκοπος is ‘scout’ (the house word), with νήεσσιν ἡμετέρῃσιν ‘for our ships’ in epic dative plurals. ἦ τινα συλήσων is the future participle of συλάω ‘strip’, and νεκύων κατατεθνηώτων is the house ‘of the dead, of those who have died’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐῶμέν μιν πρῶτα παρεξελθεῖν πεδίοιο
τυτθόν·
sentences.tr:
all’ eōmen min prōta parexelthein pedioio
tytthon·
sentences.l:
But let us allow him first to pass by across the plain
a little way;
sentences.i: But let us first let him go past us a little way across the plain;
sentences.n: ἐῶμεν is the subjunctive of ἐάω ‘allow’, ‘let us allow’, with μιν ‘him’ and the infinitive παρεξελθεῖν ‘to pass by’. πρῶτα ‘first’; πεδίοιο is a genitive of the ground crossed, ‘across the plain’; and τυτθόν is ‘a little way’. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
ἔπειτα δέ κ’ αὐτὸν ἐπαΐξαντες ἕλοιμεν
καρπαλίμως·
sentences.tr:
epeita de k’ auton epaïxantes heloimen
karpalimōs·
sentences.l:
then we could, rushing at him, take him
swiftly;
sentences.i: then we could rush at him and seize him swiftly;
sentences.n: ἔπειτα ‘then’. ἕλοιμεν is the optative with κ’ (= κεν), ‘we could take’; ἐπαΐξαντες is the aorist participle of ἐπαΐσσω ‘rushing at (him)’; and καρπαλίμως is ‘swiftly’. The unit begins in the middle of line 345 and ends at the raised dot in line 346.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἄμμε παραφθαίησι πόδεσσιν,
αἰεί μιν ἐπὶ νῆας ἀπὸ στρατόφι προτιειλεῖν
ἔγχει ἐπαΐσσων, μή πως προτὶ ἄστυ ἀλύξῃ.
sentences.tr:
ei d’ amme paraphthaiēsi podessin,
aiei min epi nēas apo stratophi protieilein
enchei epaïssōn, mē pōs proti asty alyxēi.
sentences.l:
but if he outstrips us on his feet,
always press him toward the ships away from the army,
rushing at him with your spear, lest somehow toward the town he escape.”
sentences.i: but if he outruns us on foot, keep pressing him toward the ships and away from the army, charging at him with your spear, so that he does not somehow escape toward the town.”
sentences.n: ἄμμε is ‘us’ (= ἡμᾶς, an old form) and παραφθαίησι the subjunctive of παραφθάνω, ‘gets past, outstrips’. προτιειλεῖν is an infinitive standing for a command, ‘press him’, from a rare verb meaning to drive or hem in; ἀπὸ στρατόφι ‘away from the army’ has the old ending -φι. ἔγχει ἐπαΐσσων is ‘rushing at him with the spear’. μή πως ‘lest somehow’, and ἀλύξῃ is the aorist subjunctive ‘he escape’. Odysseus’ speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσαντε παρὲξ ὁδοῦ ἐν νεκύεσσι
κλινθήτην·
sentences.tr:
hōs ara phōnēsante parex hodou en nekyessi
klinthētēn·
sentences.l:
So then, the two having spoken, aside from the road among the dead
they lay down;
sentences.i: So the two spoke, and stepping aside from the road, they lay down among the dead;
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσαντε ‘so then the two having spoken’ has an aorist dual participle. παρὲξ ὁδοῦ is ‘out of the road’, with the genitive; ἐν νεκύεσσι ‘among the dead’ has the epic dative plural. κλινθήτην is the dual aorist passive of κλίνω, ‘they laid themselves down’. The edition begins a new paragraph here, and the unit ends at the raised dot in line 350.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ ὦκα παρέδραμεν ἀφραδίῃσιν.
sentences.tr: ho d’ ar’ ōka paredramen aphradiēisin.
sentences.l: and he quickly ran past, in follies.
sentences.i: and Dolon ran quickly past in his folly.
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ ‘and he’ is Dolon. ὦκα is ‘quickly’, and παρέδραμεν ‘ran past’. ἀφραδίῃσιν is the dative plural of ἀφραδίη, the house ‘follies’ in the literal line and ‘folly’ in the free one; it gives the cause, for it is his lack of sense that keeps him from seeing the two on the ground.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ἀπέην ὅσσόν τ’ ἐπὶ οὖρα πέλονται
ἡμιόνων·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē rh’ apeēn hosson t’ epi oura pelontai
hēmionōn·
sentences.l:
But when he was as far away as, of mules,
the furrow-lengths go;
sentences.i: But when he was as far off as the length of a mule-team’s furrow;
sentences.n: The distance is told in ploughing. ἀπέην is the imperfect of ἄπειμι ‘be away’, and ἡμιόνων ‘of mules’ is a genitive. οὖρα is a rare word, evidently the length a pair of mules ploughs in one furrow (a ploughing distance); its exact length is not known. The unit ends at the raised dot, after the first word of line 352.

sentences.t:
αἱ γάρ τε βοῶν προφερέστεραί εἰσιν
ἑλκέμεναι νειοῖο βαθείης πηκτὸν ἄροτρον·
sentences.tr:
hai gar te boōn propheresterai eisin
helkemenai neioio batheiēs pēkton arotron·
sentences.l:
for they are better than oxen
at drawing the jointed plough through deep fallow land;
sentences.i: for they are better than oxen at drawing the jointed plough through deep fallow land;
sentences.n: γάρ τε gives the reason for the comparison. αἱ ‘they’ are the mules (the word ἡμίονος can be feminine); βοῶν is the genitive of comparison, ‘than oxen’; and προφερέστεραι is ‘better, superior’, with ἑλκέμεναι ‘at drawing’ (the infinitive in -έμεναι). νειοῖο βαθείης is ‘deep fallow land’ (νειός, a fallow field), and πηκτὸν ἄροτρον ‘the jointed plough’ is the Odyssey’s phrase at 13.32.

sentences.t: τὼ μὲν ἐπεδραμέτην, ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ ἔστη δοῦπον ἀκούσας.
sentences.tr: tō men epedrametēn, ho d’ ar’ estē doupon akousas.
sentences.l: the two ran up, but he stood still, a crash having heard.
sentences.i: the two ran up, but he stood still when he heard the crash.
sentences.n: τὼ μέν ‘the two’ is a dual, and ἐπεδραμέτην the dual of ἐπέδραμον ‘ran up’. ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ ἔστη is ‘and he stood still’, Dolon. δοῦπον ‘crash’ is the house word; here it is the heavy sound of the two men’s running, as the next lines show.

sentences.t:
ἔλπετο γὰρ κατὰ θυμὸν ἀποστρέψοντας ἑταίρους
ἐκ Τρώων ἰέναι πάλιν Ἕκτορος ὀτρύναντος.
sentences.tr:
elpeto gar kata thymon apostrepsontas hetairous
ek Trōōn ienai palin Hektoros otrynantos.
sentences.l:
For he hoped in his heart that companions, to turn him back,
were coming from the Trojans again, Hector having urged them on.
sentences.i: For he hoped in his heart that companions were coming back from the Trojans to turn him back, since Hector had urged them on.
sentences.n: ἔλπετο γάρ ‘for he hoped’ explains why he stopped. κατὰ θυμόν is ‘in his heart’. ἀποστρέψοντας is a future participle with ἑταίρους ‘companions’, ‘intending to turn (him) back’, the object being understood. ἰέναι πάλιν is ‘to be coming back’, and Ἕκτορος ὀτρύναντος is a genitive absolute, ‘Hector having urged them on’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ἄπεσαν δουρηνεκὲς ἢ καὶ ἔλασσον,
γνῶ ῥ’ ἄνδρας δηΐους, λαιψηρὰ δὲ γούνατ’ ἐνώμα
φευγέμεναι·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē rh’ apesan dourēnekes ē kai elasson,
gnō rh’ andras dēïous, laipsēra de gounat’ enōma
pheugemenai·
sentences.i: But when they were no more than a spear’s cast away, or even less, he knew them for enemies, and set his quick knees moving in flight;
sentences.n: ἄπεσαν is the imperfect of ἄπειμι ‘were away’, and δουρηνεκές means as far as a spear carries, a spear-cast, ἢ καὶ ἔλασσον ‘or even less’. γνῶ is the aorist of γιγνώσκω without augment. ἄνδρας δηΐους is ‘hostile men’ (δήϊος ‘hostile’), and λαιψηρά ‘quick’ describes the knees. γούνατ’ ἐνώμα is ‘he plied his knees’, νωμάω being ‘handle, ply’. The unit ends at the raised dot in line 359.

sentences.t: τοὶ δ’ αἶψα διώκειν ὁρμήθησαν.
sentences.tr: toi d’ aipsa diōkein hormēthēsan.
sentences.l: and they at once rushed to pursue.
sentences.i: and the two at once rushed to pursue him.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 359, after the raised dot. τοί here is the old plural of the demonstrative, ‘they’, the two heroes. αἶψα is ‘at once’, διώκειν ‘to pursue’, and ὁρμήθησαν the aorist passive of ὁρμάω ‘set in motion, rush’.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτε καρχαρόδοντε δύω κύνε εἰδότε θήρης
ἢ κεμάδ’ ἠὲ λαγωὸν ἐπείγετον ἐμμενὲς αἰεὶ
χῶρον ἀν’ ὑλήενθ’, ὃ δέ τε προθέῃσι μεμηκώς,
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hote karcharodonte dyō kyne eidote thērēs
ē kemad’ ēe lagōon epeigeton emmenes aiei
chōron an’ hylēenth’, ho de te protheēisi memēkōs,
sentences.l:
And as when two sharp-toothed dogs, skilled in the hunt,
either a young deer or a hare press hard, steadily, always,
through a wooded place, and it runs on ahead, bleating,
sentences.i: And as when two sharp-toothed hounds, skilled in the hunt, press a young deer or a hare hard and steadily, without pause, through wooded country, while it runs on ahead, bleating,
sentences.n: A simile begins: ὡς δ’ ὅτε ‘and as when’, answered by ὣς in line 363. καρχαρόδοντε … κύνε is a dual, ‘two sharp-toothed dogs’, and εἰδότε θήρης ‘skilled in the hunt’. κεμάς is a young deer (some take it as a hornless one; the exact sense is not certain), λαγωός ‘hare’, and ἐπείγετον ‘press hard’. ἐμμενὲς αἰεί is ‘steadily, always’. ὑλήενθ’ is ‘wooded’, and μεμηκώς, from μηκάομαι, ‘bleating’, belongs to the hunted animal. The unit is cut at the comma, since the sentence runs five lines.

sentences.t:
ὣς τὸν Τυδεΐδης ἠδ’ ὃ πτολίπορθος Ὀδυσσεὺς
λαοῦ ἀποτμήξαντε διώκετον ἐμμενὲς αἰεί.
sentences.tr:
hōs ton Tydeïdēs ēd’ ho ptoliporthos Odysseus
laou apotmēxante diōketon emmenes aiei.
sentences.l:
so him Tydeus’-son and he, the city-sacking Odysseus,
having cut him off from the people, pursued steadily, always.
sentences.i: so the son of Tydeus and Odysseus, the city-sacker, cut him off from the army and pursued him steadily, without pause.
sentences.n: ὣς answers the simile. τὸν ‘him’ is Dolon, Τυδεΐδης ‘son of Tydeus’ is Diomedes, and πτολίπορθος Ὀδυσσεύς is the house ‘city-sacking Odysseus’, with ὃ as a stress on the epithet. ἀποτμήξαντε is a dual aorist participle of ἀποτμήγω ‘cut off’, with λαοῦ ‘from the people’; διώκετον is the dual ‘pursued’. ἐμμενὲς αἰεί repeats the words of the simile, and the English matches.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ τάχ’ ἔμελλε μιγήσεσθαι φυλάκεσσι
φεύγων ἐς νῆας, τότε δὴ μένος ἔμβαλ’ Ἀθήνη
Τυδεΐδῃ, ἵνα μή τις Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων
φθαίη ἐπευξάμενος βαλέειν, ὃ δὲ δεύτερος ἔλθοι.
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē tach’ emelle migēsesthai phylakessi
pheugōn es nēas, tote dē menos embal’ Athēnē
Tydeïdēi, hina mē tis Achaiōn chalkochitōnōn
phthaiē epeuxamenos baleein, ho de deuteros elthoi.
sentences.l:
But when he was soon about to mingle with the guards,
fleeing to the ships, then indeed Athena cast might into
Tydeus’-son, so that none of the bronze-shirted Achaeans
might be first to vaunt that he had struck him, and he come second.
sentences.i: But when he was just about to mingle with the guards as he fled to the ships, then Athena put might into the son of Tydeus, so that none of the bronze-shirted Achaeans could be first to cry out in triumph that he had struck the man, leaving Diomedes to come second.
sentences.n: τάχ’ ἔμελλε μιγήσεσθαι: ἔμελλε with a future infinitive is ‘was about to’, τάχα ‘soon’, and φυλάκεσσι the epic dative plural ‘the guards’. μένος ἔμβαλ’ is ‘put might into’ (μένος is ‘might’ in the Iliad). φθαίη is the aorist optative of φθάνω ‘get in first’, and ἐπευξάμενος here is ‘vaunting’ (‘crying out in triumph’ in the free English, as ἐπεύχεται at 5.119), not ‘praying’. ὃ δὲ δεύτερος ἔλθοι is ‘and he come second’, Diomedes. χαλκοχιτώνων is the house ‘bronze-shirted’.

sentences.t: δουρὶ δ’ ἐπαΐσσων προσέφη κρατερὸς Διομήδης·
sentences.tr: douri d’ epaïssōn prosephē krateros Diomēdēs·
sentences.l: And with his spear rushing at him addressed strong Diomedes:
sentences.i: Charging at him with his spear, strong Diomedes spoke:
sentences.n: δουρὶ δ’ ἐπαΐσσων is ‘rushing at him with his spear’, with the dative of the weapon. προσέφη is ‘addressed’, and κρατερὸς Διομήδης ‘strong Diomedes’ is the house epithet pair (κρατερός ‘strong’). The unit introduces Diomedes’ shout.

sentences.t:
ἠὲ μέν’ ἠέ σε δουρὶ κιχήσομαι, οὐδέ σέ φημι
δηρὸν ἐμῆς ἀπὸ χειρὸς ἀλύξειν αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον.
sentences.tr:
ēe men’ ēe se douri kichēsomai, oude se phēmi
dēron emēs apo cheiros alyxein aipyn olethron.
sentences.l:
“Either stand, or with my spear I shall reach you, and I say you will not
long from my hand escape steep destruction.”
sentences.i: “Either stand still, or I shall reach you with my spear; and I tell you that you will not long escape steep destruction at my hand.”
sentences.n: Diomedes shouts to the fugitive. ἠὲ μέν’ ἠέ σε …: μέν’ is μένε ‘stand, wait’, the imperative, ‘either stand, or’; κιχήσομαι is the future of κιχάνω ‘reach’, with δουρί ‘with my spear’. οὐδέ σέ φημι … ἀλύξειν is ‘and I say that you will not escape’ (future infinitive of ἀλύσκω). δηρόν ‘for long’, ἐμῆς ἀπὸ χειρός ‘from my hand’, αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον the house ‘steep destruction’.

sentences.t: ἦ ῥα καὶ ἔγχος ἀφῆκεν, ἑκὼν δ’ ἡμάρτανε φωτός·
sentences.tr: ē rha kai enchos aphēken, hekōn d’ hēmartane phōtos·
sentences.l: He spoke, and let fly his spear, and willingly he missed the man;
sentences.i: So he said, and let fly his spear, but missed the man on purpose;
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα καὶ ‘he spoke, and’ is the usual formula after a speech; ἦ is a past tense of ἠμί ‘say’. ἔγχος ἀφῆκεν is ‘let fly his spear’. ἑκών ‘willingly, on purpose’ tells us that Diomedes meant to miss, and ἡμάρτανε is the imperfect of ἁμαρτάνω ‘miss’, with the genitive φωτός ‘the man’. The edition begins a new paragraph here.

sentences.t:
δεξιτερὸν δ’ ὑπὲρ ὦμον ἐΰξου δουρὸς ἀκωκὴ
ἐν γαίῃ ἐπάγη·
sentences.tr:
dexiteron d’ hyper ōmon eÿxou douros akōkē
en gaiēi epagē·
sentences.l:
and over his right shoulder the point of the well-polished spear
in the earth stuck fast;
sentences.i: and the point of the well-polished spear stuck fast in the earth above his right shoulder;
sentences.n: The spear passes ὑπὲρ ὦμον ‘over the shoulder’ (δεξιτερόν ‘right’). ἐΰξου, from ἐΰξοος, is ‘well-polished’ (the house word), ἀκωκή ‘point’, ἐν γαίῃ ‘in the earth’, and ἐπάγη the second aorist passive of πήγνυμι ‘was fixed’. The unit ends at the raised dot in line 374.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ ἔστη τάρβησέν τε
βαμβαίνων·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ ar’ estē tarbēsen te
bambainōn·
sentences.l:
and he stood still and was terrified,
stammering;
sentences.i: and he stood still, terrified and stammering;
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ ἔστη is ‘and he stood still’, Dolon; τάρβησεν is the aorist of ταρβέω ‘be terrified’. βαμβαίνων is a rare participle apparently imitating the sound of chattering; ‘stammering’ is a guess, and the exact meaning (stammer, chatter, totter) is not known. The unit begins in the middle of line 374 and ends at the raised dot in line 375.

sentences.t: ἄραβος δὲ διὰ στόμα γίγνετ’ ὀδόντων·
sentences.tr: arabos de dia stoma gignet’ odontōn·
sentences.l: and a clatter came about through his mouth, of his teeth;
sentences.i: and his teeth began to clatter in his mouth;
sentences.n: ἄραβος is a rare noun for a clatter or rattle, apparently imitating the sound; its derivation is not known. It is the clatter ὀδόντων ‘of the teeth’, and διὰ στόμα ‘through the mouth’ gives its place. γίγνετ’ is γίγνετο, an imperfect, ‘was coming about’. The unit begins in the middle of line 375.

sentences.t: χλωρὸς ὑπαὶ δείους·
sentences.tr: chlōros hypai deious·
sentences.l: pale beneath fear;
sentences.i: pale with fear;
sentences.n: A short clause that goes with the picture of Dolon. χλωρός is the house ‘pale’ (elsewhere it can mean green or yellow); ὑπαί is ὑπό ‘under’, and δείους is the genitive of δέος ‘fear’, so ‘pale from fear’. The unit is the first words of line 376, to the raised dot.

sentences.t:
τὼ δ’ ἀσθμαίνοντε κιχήτην,
χειρῶν δ’ ἁψάσθην·
sentences.tr:
tō d’ asthmainonte kichētēn,
cheirōn d’ hapsasthēn·
sentences.l:
and the two, panting, reached him,
and of his hands took hold;
sentences.i: the two reached him, panting, and took hold of his hands;
sentences.n: τὼ δ’ ‘and the two’ is a dual, as are ἀσθμαίνοντε ‘panting’ and κιχήτην ‘reached (him)’, the aorist of κιχάνω. χειρῶν ἁψάσθην is ‘took hold of his hands’, the genitive going with the aorist dual of ἅπτομαι. The unit ends at the raised dot in line 377.

sentences.t: ὃ δὲ δακρύσας ἔπος ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ho de dakrysas epos ēuda·
sentences.l: and he, in tears, spoke a word:
sentences.i: and he said, in tears:
sentences.n: ὃ δέ ‘and he’ is Dolon. δακρύσας is the aorist participle of δακρύω ‘weep’, here ‘in tears’, and ἔπος ηὔδα is ‘spoke a word’ (ηὔδα the imperfect of αὐδάω ‘speak’). The line leads into his plea.

sentences.t: ζωγρεῖτ’, αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν ἐμὲ λύσομαι·
sentences.tr: zōgreit’, autar egōn eme lysomai·
sentences.l: “Take me alive, and I shall ransom myself;
sentences.i: “Take me alive, and I will ransom myself;
sentences.n: Dolon pleads, with no quotation marks in the Greek. ζωγρεῖτ’ (= ζωγρεῖτε) is the plural imperative of ζωγρέω ‘take alive’, with ‘me’ understood. αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν ἐμὲ λύσομαι is ‘but I myself shall ransom myself’: ἐγών is an epic form of ἐγώ, and λύσομαι the future middle of λύω ‘loose’, here ‘ransom’. The unit ends at the raised dot in line 378.

sentences.t:
ἔστι γὰρ ἔνδον
χαλκός τε χρυσός τε πολύκμητός τε σίδηρος,
τῶν κ’ ὔμμιν χαρίσαιτο πατὴρ ἀπερείσι’ ἄποινα
εἴ κεν ἐμὲ ζωὸν πεπύθοιτ’ ἐπὶ νηυσὶν Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
esti gar endon
chalkos te chrysos te polykmētos te sidēros,
tōn k’ ymmin charisaito patēr apereisi’ apoina
ei ken eme zōon pepythoit’ epi nēusin Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
for there is within
bronze and gold and much-laboured iron,
of these my father would grant you unstinted ransom,
if me alive he should learn of at the ships of the Achaeans.”
sentences.i: for inside there are bronze and gold and iron worked with much labour. From these my father would grant you an unstinted ransom, if he were to learn that I am alive at the ships of the Achaeans.”
sentences.n: He names the ransom: ἔστι γάρ ‘for there is’ and ἔνδον ‘within’, in his father’s house. Lines 379 and 381 are 6.48 and 6.50 word for word, and 380 is 6.49 with ὔμμιν ‘to you’ (= ὑμῖν, plural) for τοι, so the English is that of 6.48–50. πολύκμητος ‘much-laboured’ comes from κάμνω ‘toil’; ἀπερείσι’ ἄποινα is the house ‘unstinted ransom’; πεπύθοιτο is the optative of πυνθάνομαι ‘learn’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him:
sentences.n: The reply formula: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη is ‘him answering addressed’ (ἀπαμειβόμενος from ἀπαμείβομαι ‘answer’). πολύμητις is the house epithet of Odysseus, ‘of many wiles’ (μῆτις is ‘cunning’). The line is also in the Odyssey and takes that English. The edition begins a new paragraph here.

sentences.t: θάρσει, μηδέ τί τοι θάνατος καταθύμιος ἔστω.
sentences.tr: tharsei, mēde ti toi thanatos katathymios estō.
sentences.l: “Take courage, and let death not at all be in-your-heart for you.
sentences.i: “Take courage, and do not let death be on your mind at all.
sentences.n: Odysseus answers. θάρσει is the imperative ‘take courage’ (θαρσέω). μηδέ τί τοι … ἔστω is ‘and let not at all … be’, with τοι ‘for you’ and θάνατος ‘death’. καταθύμιος is built on κατά and θυμός, ‘in the heart’, that is on the mind, as in the Odyssey’s τό μοι καταθύμιόν ἐστιν. The sentence ends at the full stop, and no reason is given for the comfort.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι τόδε εἰπὲ καὶ ἀτρεκέως κατάλεξον·
sentences.tr: all’ age moi tode eipe kai atrekeōs katalexon·
sentences.l: But come, tell me this, and recount it exactly;
sentences.i: But come now, tell me this, and set it out for me exactly:
sentences.n: This line is word for word Odyssey 1.169 and takes that English. ἀλλ’ ἄγε ‘but come’ opens an order; εἰπέ is the aorist imperative ‘tell’ (from εἶπον), and κατάλεξον the aorist imperative of καταλέγω ‘recount’. ἀτρεκέως is ‘exactly’ (not ‘truly’, which is another word).

sentences.t:
πῇ δὴ οὕτως ἐπὶ νῆας ἀπὸ στρατοῦ ἔρχεαι οἶος
νύκτα δι’ ὀρφναίην, ὅτε θ’ εὕδουσι βροτοὶ ἄλλοι;
sentences.tr:
pēi dē houtōs epi nēas apo stratou ercheai oios
nykta di’ orphnaiēn, hote th’ heudousi brotoi alloi;
sentences.l:
Whither, then, thus to the ships from the army do you go alone
through the murky night, when other mortals sleep?
sentences.i: Where are you going like this, alone, from the army toward the ships, in the murky night when other mortals sleep?
sentences.n: Odysseus begins his questions. πῇ δὴ οὕτως is ‘whither, then, in this way’, and ἔρχεαι is the second person ἔρχῃ ‘you go’, with οἶος ‘alone’. The second line, νύκτα δι’ ὀρφναίην, ὅτε θ’ εὕδουσι βροτοὶ ἄλλοι, is also 10.83 (Nestor’s question to Agamemnon), so ‘the murky night’ and ‘other mortals’ are the English of that line. The unit ends at the question mark (;).

sentences.t: ἤ τινα συλήσων νεκύων κατατεθνηώτων;
sentences.tr: ē tina sylēsōn nekyōn katatethnēōtōn;
sentences.l: or going to strip someone of the dead, of those who have died?
sentences.i: Or are you on your way to strip one of the dead?
sentences.n: This is Odysseus’ own guess of line 343 put to Dolon, with ἤ for ἦ and a question mark for the full stop; the same words get the same English. ἤ … ‘or’ is the first alternative, and συλήσων is the future participle of συλάω ‘strip’, ‘going to strip’.

sentences.t:
ἦ σ’ Ἕκτωρ προέηκε διασκοπιᾶσθαι ἕκαστα
νῆας ἔπι γλαφυράς;
sentences.tr:
ē s’ Hektōr proeēke diaskopiasthai hekasta
nēas epi glaphyras;
sentences.l:
Or did Hector send you forth to spy out each thing
at the hollow ships?
sentences.i: Or did Hector send you out to spy out everything at the hollow ships?
sentences.n: ἦ here is ‘or’, the next alternative. σ’ is σε ‘you’, and προέηκε is the aorist of προΐημι ‘send forth’. διασκοπιᾶσθαι is ‘to spy out’ (from σκοπιάομαι), ἕκαστα ‘each thing, every detail’, and νῆας ἔπι γλαφυράς ‘at the hollow ships’ has ἔπι after its noun; γλαφυρός is the house ‘hollow’. The unit ends at the question mark in line 389.

sentences.t: ἦ σ’ αὐτὸν θυμὸς ἀνῆκε;
sentences.tr: ē s’ auton thymos anēke;
sentences.l: Or did your own heart urge you on?”
sentences.i: Or did your own heart urge you on?”
sentences.n: The last alternative: ἦ ‘or’, σ’ αὐτόν ‘you yourself’, θυμός ‘heart’ and ἀνῆκε ‘urged on’ (from ἀνίημι, whose house word is ‘urge on’). Odysseus’ speech ends here, and Dolon’s answer opens the next part.
